Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds. Fix $L>0$ as the numerical period in the declared SI metre unit, so the physical side length is $L\,\mathrm m$, and use the flat periodic cell $\mathbb T_L^3=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$ with normalized spatial measure $L^{-3}dx$. Spatial coordinates in physical volume integrals are measured in metres. Assume Countable Choice for the stated Fourier and Sobolev space conventions. The velocity is a vector field $u:I\times\mathbb T_L^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with SI units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the mass density is a constant primitive parameter $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; the dynamic viscosity is a constant primitive parameter $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$; and the mechanical pressure $p$ has units $\mathrm{Pa}$. The body-force density is zero (its SI unit is $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$), and there is no temperature variable in this model.

For classical fields take $u\in C^1(I;C^2(\mathbb T_L^3;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p\in C^1(I;C^1(\mathbb T_L^3))$. Adopt incompressibility $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and the local momentum balance
$$\rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)\bigr)=\operatorname{div}\sigma,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D(u),\qquad D(u)=\tfrac12\bigl(\nabla u+(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}\bigr).$$
Here $\sigma$ is the Cauchy stress, so its traction on an oriented surface with unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$; $D(u)$ is the symmetric rate-of-deformation tensor; and $\nabla$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Every term in the momentum balance has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, this equation is equivalently
$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nabla\pi=\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nu=\mu/\rho_0>0,\qquad \pi=p/\rho_0.$$
where kinematic viscosity $\nu$ and kinematic pressure $\pi$ have units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, respectively. All fields are periodic in each spatial coordinate; this is an ideal cell, not a wall-bounded vessel.

For the weak regime, use the global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf class. The spaces are $H$, the real $L^2$ vector fields whose divergence vanishes distributionally on $\mathbb T_L^3$, with unrestricted constant Fourier mode, and $V=H\cap H^1$, where $H^1$ consists of fields and first weak derivatives in $L^2$; use normalized spatial norms. Here $C_w([0,\infty);H)$ means that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$; the time-dependent $L^p$ spaces are the corresponding Bochner spaces. A weak velocity has $u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$, strongly attains $u_0\in H$ as $t\downarrow0$, and satisfies, for every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field $\phi$ compactly supported in time,
$$
\int_0^\infty\!\bigl[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\bigr]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.
$$
The tensor pairing is $L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i\,dx$, and the gradient pairing is $L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i\,dx$. The class also requires
$$
\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2\qquad(t\ge0),
$$
and a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that
$$
\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2\qquad(s\in S\cup\{0\},\ t\ge s).
$$
This weak convention asserts neither uniqueness nor pressure regularity. These equations and the solution class are adopted model assumptions; they are not deductions that every physical fluid obeys them.

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf
solution** with data $(\nu,u_0)$ is a map
$u:[0,\infty)\to H$ such that its restriction to each finite interval is in
$C_w([0,T];H)$ and its Bochner equivalence classes satisfy
$u\in L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$. All clauses
involving $u(t)$ at a specified time, including the initial trace and energy
inequalities, refer to this weakly continuous map. By the uniqueness result in

representative of those Bochner classes. It must satisfy $u(0)=u_0$ in $H$,
$\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and for
every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field
$\phi:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ compactly supported in
time,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It must also satisfy, for every $t\ge0$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2,$$
and there must be a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for
every $s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and every $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
For a matrix field $A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The tensor pairing means $(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$;
the gradient pairing means $\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$.
All derivatives in the weak identity are distributional; the definition
asserts neither uniqueness nor smoothness.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the periodic solenoidal
Fourier spaces defined above. Then there
exists a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$
under the definition above. This is an existence assertion; it asserts no
uniqueness or global smoothness.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For a vector $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb T^3$ define the **character**
$$e_k(x):=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(k_1x_1+k_2x_2+k_3x_3)\bigr)=e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot x},$$
where each $x_j$ is inserted through any real representative and $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]); the definition does not depend on the representatives. Then $|e_k(x)|=1$, $e_k e_l=e_{k+l}$, and $e_{-k}=\overline{e_k}$.

Similarly $L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ denotes the integrable complex vector fields.

**Fourier coefficients.** For $u\in L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ define
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(x)\,e_{-k}(x)\,dx\ \in\mathbb C^3 .$$
The integral depends only on the class of $u$. A field $u\in L^1$ is real almost everywhere if and only if $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; the forward direction uses $\widehat{\overline u}(k)=\overline{\widehat u(-k)}$, and the reverse uses $L^1$ Fourier uniqueness, proved below. On the circle this uniqueness follows from [[thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp]] with $p=1$: zero coefficients give zero Fejer means, whose $L^1$ limit is the function. To pass to $\mathbb T^d$ for $d=2,3$, use [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for fixed $k'\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, $g_{k'}(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-1}}u(x_1,x')e_{-k'}(x')dx'$ is in $L^1(\mathbb T)$ and all its coefficients vanish. Hence $g_{k'}=0$ almost everywhere. The countable union of the exceptional sets over $k'$ is null. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. Apply this uniqueness to $u-\overline u$ to obtain the reverse real-valuedness implication. **Weights.** For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ set
$$w_k:=\bigl(1+|2\pi k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}\ \ge 1,$$
so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$

For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$

$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$

$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$

$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
